summary: This is a JSTOR catalog page for Leon Wansleben's 2023 Harvard University Press book The Rise of Central Banks: State Power in Financial Capitalism, a 336-page work. The page shows the table of contents and chapter excerpts. The book argues that central banks grew more powerful since the 1970s by using infrastructural power tied to financialized, market-based finance, contrasting German and Swiss conservative institutions with Anglo-Saxon market-based approaches.
one_line: JSTOR catalog page for Leon Wansleben's 2023 book on how central banks rose to power in financial capitalism since the 1970s.
key_facts: The Rise of Central Banks: State Power in Financial Capitalism is written by Leon Wansleben and published by Harvard University Press in 2023.
The book has 336 pages and its DOI is 10.2307/j.ctv32nxzdq.
In July 1972, Helmut Schmidt, Germany's finance minister and later Chancellor, proclaimed that higher inflation was tolerable because people cared more about retaining their jobs.
Two months later, Schmidt admitted that "[o]ur economic policy is much more limited than our old textbooks used to tell."
Chapter One is titled Neoliberalism and the Rise of Central Banks and spans pages 23-67.
Chapter Two is titled Monetarism and the Invention of Monetary Policy and spans pages 68-106.
Chapter Three is titled Hegemonizing Financial Market Expectations and spans pages 107-142.
Chapter Four argues there is a recursive causality between the global integration of money markets and the spread of inflation targeting.
Chapter Five is titled The Organization of Ignorance: How Central Bankers Abandoned Regulation and spans pages 175-205.
Chapter Six is titled Plumbing Financialization in Vain: Central Banking after 2008 and spans pages 206-227.
The Conclusion states that Anglo-Saxon central bankers taught the world how to capitalize on the globalizing logic of market-based finance.
The Conclusion says German and Swiss infrastructural power came from universal banking and corporatist wage coordination.
The book's introduction notes that the Keynesian compromise between social democracy and private capital seemed broken in the late 1960s and 1970s.
